s01.ttsText: [softly] Agra. August, sixteen sixty-six. Around one house in the Mughal city, a ring of guards stands watch. One letter from Agra puts that watch at a thousand men. Inside are a Maratha ruler from the Deccan... and his nine-year-old son. [tense] Then, one morning, word races through the city. [whispers] They are gone.

s02.ttsText: [curious] How do you vanish from under the eyes of one of the richest empires on earth? You may know the famous answer. Baskets of sweets. But letters written in Agra that very summer still survive. So let's check the legend... against the record.

s03.ttsText: First, the players. Shivaji: the Maratha leader who carved a kingdom out of the hill forts of western India, and spent years raiding Mughal territory. Facing him, the emperor, Aurangzeb. And the man who would bring them face to face... Aurangzeb's veteran general, Mirza Raja Jai Singh.

s04.ttsText: In sixteen sixty-five, Jai Singh's army closed in on Shivaji's forts. Rather than lose everything, Shivaji made a deal at Purandar. Twenty-three forts went to the empire. He kept twelve, including his stronghold, Rajgad. But Jai Singh wanted more. Shivaji should travel north, and stand before the emperor in person. Jai Singh swore that no harm would come to him. And at court, his son, the prince Ram Singh, gave his word as well. [serious] Remember that promise.

s05.ttsText: In March sixteen sixty-six, Shivaji set out from Rajgad with his son, Sambhaji, and a small but splendid escort. In May, they reached Agra. One of Ram Singh's officers described him in a letter home. Lean. Short. Fair. Bearded. [warmly] And, he wrote, "even without finding out who he is, one does feel instinctively that he is a ruler of men."

s06.ttsText: The twelfth of May. The emperor's fiftieth birthday, by the lunar calendar. Ram Singh led Shivaji into the fort. Shivaji presented his gifts of gold... and waited. [softly] Nothing. The emperor did not say a single word to him. Shivaji was led back, to stand behind rows of other nobles. Then robes of honour went to princes, to ministers... and to Maharaja Jaswant Singh, a general who had once besieged one of Shivaji's forts... and failed.

s07.ttsText: [tense] For Shivaji, it was too much. According to a letter from Ram Singh's staff, he told the prince, "I cast off your mun-sub." His imperial rank. Then he turned his back on the throne... and walked away. At a court where nobles were expected to wait, as one English trader put it, "with their hands before them, like mutes," it was a stunning act of defiance. Officials brought him a robe of honour. He refused it.

s08.ttsText: [serious] Now the court turned on him. Powerful voices, the emperor's own sister, Jahanara, among them, demanded punishment. A letter from Agra reports that the emperor weighed his options. Kill Shivaji... or lock him away in a fortress. Then Ram Singh stepped in. His father had guaranteed Shivaji's safety, he argued. If the emperor wanted Shivaji dead, he would have to kill Ram Singh first. The emperor's answer was simple. Then sign a security bond. If Shivaji escapes... you will answer for it.

s09.ttsText: Ram Singh signed. Shivaji was not executed... but he was not free. At one point, he was ordered to march to Kabul, on the far north-western frontier. Days later, after petitions, and payments to courtiers, the order was dropped. Troops of the city's police chief, Fulad Khan, ringed his quarters. Ram Singh's own Rajputs watched his bed at night. [softly] The emperor's guest... had become his prisoner.

s10.ttsText: So Shivaji tried everything. Two crore rupees, twenty million, if his forts were returned. An offer to fight for the emperor against Bijapur. He even asked to go to Benares, and become a holy man. The reply came back. Let him become a fakir, then... and live in Allahabad fort, under guard.

s11.ttsText: [serious] And then came a blow from the very man who had promised his safety. In July, Jai Singh wrote to his son from the Deccan. It was, he said, "not at all politic" to let Shivaji come home. Keep him in Agra. Treat him well... but keep him. Shivaji's money was running out. He borrowed sixty-six thousand rupees from Ram Singh. And over the summer, he sent his own escort home, leaving himself almost alone. To the court, it looked like surrender.

s12.ttsText: [curious] It wasn't surrender. It was preparation. Shivaji fell ill... or seemed to. Soon, large baskets of sweets began to leave his quarters. Gifts for Brahmins, holy men, and courtiers. Each one hung from a pole, carried by two porters. At first, the guards opened them, and found sweets. After a few days... they stopped opening them.

s13.ttsText: [whispers] Then, one evening in the third week of August, the plan goes into motion. [softly] According to later accounts, Shivaji's half-brother, Hiroji Farzand, lies down on Shivaji's bed, under a quilt. One arm is left showing, with Shivaji's gold bracelet on the wrist. A boy sits by the bed, massaging his feet. And inside the baskets, among others filled with real sweets, crouch Shivaji... and his son. The porters lift the poles. They walk past the guards. [whispers] And out... into the dark.

s14.ttsText: [curious] How long did the trick hold? The chronicles say the guards were fooled for most of the next day, until the house fell strangely quiet, and they found the bed empty. The letters written at the time suggest it was quicker. One, written in Agra and dated the eighteenth of August, says simply: "This morning Shivaji was found to have fled."

s15.ttsText: [tense] Agra erupted. Ram Singh's own staff wrote home, urging that every pass and river crossing be watched, and that anyone dressed as a yogi or a sun-yaasi be questioned and searched. Fulad Khan, whose men had ringed the house, told the emperor the escape had happened on Ram Singh's side of the watch. Ram Singh's men were seized and threatened until they said their master had helped. Some later took it back. The emperor, furious, cut Ram Singh's rank and took away his lands.

s16.ttsText: [curious] So... was it really the baskets? About two weeks after the escape, one of Ram Singh's officers wrote that the trick had become known. Shivaji had slipped out "by crouching down in the baskets." Later Mughal and Maratha histories tell the same story. But the Mughal court suspected inside help, too. And a European writer of the time, Niccolao Manoochi, claimed that Ram Singh himself had quietly arranged it. [softly] With frightened guards and partisan witnesses, we may never know exactly who looked the other way.

s17.ttsText: What happened next... grew into legend. For generations, Shivaji's flight was told as a long pilgrimage, through Benares, Gaya, even Puri. The chronicles say he smeared himself with ash, disguised as a wandering ascetic. [serious] But in nineteen thirty-nine, letters were found in the Jaipur archives. Spy reports quoted in them said Shivaji reached his fort just twenty-five days after slipping out of Agra. The historian Jaadunaath Sarkar, who had once told the long version himself, now called those pilgrimage stories fiction. Twenty-five days, over more than a thousand kilometres, meant hard, fast travel on hidden paths. [softly] And it cost him. He lay ill for weeks after he got home.

s18.ttsText: [softly] And the boy? What became of Sambhaji? Maratha accounts say he was left behind in Muthura, with a trusted Brahmin family. The spy reports that reached the emperor even said that Shivaji's son had died on the road. That rumour... may have protected him. Months later, Sambhaji travelled home in disguise, passed off as a young relative of the family sheltering him.

s19.ttsText: The escape changed the course of the Deccan wars. Within four years, Shivaji was taking back the forts he had surrendered at Purandar. In sixteen seventy-four, he was crowned Chhatrapati at Rai-gad. And in a collection of sayings attributed to Aurangzeb, the emperor laments that one moment of carelessness, the flight of Shivaji, dragged him into campaigns that lasted to the end of his days. [softly] One night. A few baskets of sweets.

s20.ttsText: [warmly] And Ram Singh? The prince who paid for the escape with his rank was later sent east, to lead a Mughal army into Assam. There, in sixteen seventy-one, on the Brahmaputra at Sarai Ghaat, he would face an Ahom general named Lachit Borphukan. [softly] But that... is a story for another episode.
